title.narrative: ROAP/PAK04/S1-810/Harmonizing Afghan Refugees and Host Communities in Urban Slums in Pakistan for Peaceful Coexistence and Social, Gender-positive Inclusiveness

description.narrative: According to the UNHCR, there are approximately three million Afghans living in Pakistan, of which 1.32 million are Proof of Registration (PoR) cardholders , approximately 840,000 hold an Afghan Citizen Card (ACC), and an estimated 775,000 are undocumented. UNHCR 2022 data show that, 53.5% of the registered Afghan refugees are male and 46.5% female. The Provinces of Baluchistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa host the vast majority (81%) of the current Afghan population in the country. There is significant concentration in other major cities including in Islamabad and also in Karachi. Some 31% of refugees live in refugee villages, and the remaining 69% live in urban, peri-urban, and rural areas alongside host communities. According to IOM, about 20% of the Afghan ACC holders in Pakistan live in refugee villages. Most Afghan refugees in Pakistan face extremely high levels of multi-dimensional poverty. More than half are counted as extremely poor and ultra-poor. The IOM data show that 31% have temporary/ad hoc employment and 52% live on less than the minimum wage supporting an average family size of six. Afghan refugees and Afghans of other status in Pakistan have several multifaceted protection needs. These include the need for access to registration and documentation to ensure basic rights, facilitate access to services and to mitigate the risk of arrest and detention. The health, housing and social-economic status of the host communities in urban slums and the Afghan refugees are generally equally very bad. Respiratory tract infections are prevalent in about half of the Afghan refugee population. The incidence rates for diarrhoea and dysentery are reported at levels of 3.49 and 1.26 out of 1,000 Afghan refugees. Housing challenges include tenure insecurity, overcrowding, rising rents, bad infrastructure and basic services. In both contexts, rising energy costs and the impacts of climate change , Where Afghan families have constructed their own homes with local materials, challenges include poor weatherproofing. Living conditions are particularly wanting for housebound household members, including the elderly and chronically ill, young children and women . Most Afghan male workers are in lowest-wage and vulnerable jobs as garbage collectors or unskilled building construction labourers. As Pakistan is experiencing a construction boom, particularly in urban areas, unskilled Afghan miss out on labour opportunities; skilled construction labour can earn 2 times the daily rates of unskilled labour. The broader urban development challenges of cities in Pakistan obviously are challenging as well. Planning and service delivery is hampered by high levels of urban population growth and urban expansion. Urban governance capacity and institutional reform have not kept pace. Municipal service delivery including on water, sanitation, waste collection and power supply cannot keep up with urban growth. Especially slum areas, which are anyhow very poorly documented in government statistics, remain chronically underserviced. Appropriate planning and service delivery requires expertise in analysing urban informal.
